title: Applying Fowler's FH(Q) criterion to torsion lattices
question: Fowler's FH(\mathbb Q) condition asks for a proper cocompact \Gamma-complex whose isotropy lies in a family \mathcal F and whose fixed-point Euler characteristics vanish. Let \Gamma be a torsion lattice acting on X=G/K with finite stabilizers. Assuming that every finite subgroup H\subset\Gamma has \chi(X^H)=0 for H\ne\{1\}, why does Fowler's theorem place \Gamma in FH(\mathbb Q)?
answer: The FH(\mathbb Q) property means that \Gamma admits a finite \Gamma-CW complex Y such that every cell stabilizer is finite and whose Bredon homology with coefficients in \mathbb Q is finitely generated in each degree. Fowler constructs Y from X by attaching finitely many equivariant cells to kill the compactly supported homology of each fixed-point set X^H. The hypotheses that X is contractible, the action is proper cocompact, and \chi(X^H)=0 for nontrivial H imply that all obstruction groups vanish, so the cellular chain complex C_*^{\mathcal F}(Y;\mathbb Q) becomes finite.\n\nConcretely, the spectral sequence with E^1_{p,q}=\bigoplus_{[\sigma]} H_q(\Gamma_{\sigma};\mathbb Q) collapses because \Gamma_{\sigma} is finite and the Euler vanishing forces acyclicity above degree 0. The resulting Bredon chain complex for Y provides a finite projective resolution of the constant functor \underline{\mathbb Q}, so \Gamma\in FH(\mathbb Q). This is the equivariant finiteness conclusion used to show that torsion lattices admit finite rational orbicomplex models even though they need not be fundamental groups of manifolds.
